title: Dearer than wealth
hookLine: Maitreyi turns down a fortune to ask about the self
carry: the innermost self is dearest of all
tomorrow: a voice from a burning bush says 'I AM.' how close is that?
last: THE TRAIL ALL ELSE IS FOUND BY.

cards: Moving day. The car is full, the trunk won't close, and something has to stay behind: the beanbag, the box of old notebooks, the poster that's been up since middle school.
Choosing what can't come is a small grief all its own. The Brihadaranyaka tells of a woman who faced a far bigger version of that choice, and chose in a way nobody expected. Her name is Maitreyi.

teach.b: You may remember her. The sage Yajnavalkya is about to leave household life, and he offers to divide all he owns between his two wives. Maitreyi asks one question.
If this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, would it make me deathless? No, he says. Your life would be like the life of the rich, and that's all.
Then what would I do with it, she says. Tell me what you know. And he tells her something startling.
It isn't for love of a husband that a husband is dear, but for love of the self.

teach.h: DEAR FOR THE SAKE OF THE SELF.
teach.b: It isn't for love of sons that sons are dear, or for wealth's sake that wealth is dear, but for love of the self. On first hearing that sounds selfish.
Teachers of Vedanta read it the other way round: the self here isn't the ego.
It's the innermost, the atman. A few verses before aham brahmasmi, the same Upanishad puts it as a ranking.

teach.h: DEARER THAN A SON, THAN WEALTH.
teach.b: This self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than anything, because it is innermost. Whoever holds something else as dearest can lose it. Whoever holds the self as dear, what they hold dear does not perish.
That isn't a promise that nothing will be lost. Things go. People move.
The beanbag stays on the curb.
It's a claim about where the love was coming from all along. And aham brahmasmi names that innermost self: Brahman.

how: Vedanta teachers read Yajnavalkya's words to Maitreyi, and the Brihadaranyaka's line on the self as dearest, as pointing to the innermost self, not to selfishness; Advaita students learn them through hearing, reflecting and meditating.

o: I am Brahman: the self is the one reality
I hold Brahman: a promise for hard times
I love Brahman: a line from a love song

p: no: a rich life, nothing more
dearer than a son, than wealth

s: this verse tells people to love themselves more than their family
as Vedanta teachers read it, the self here is the innermost, the atman, not the ego; everything dear is dear to it.
Maitreyi asked whether a whole earth full of wealth would make her deathless
Yajnavalkya said no: her life would be like the life of the rich, so she asked to be taught instead.
the verse promises that nothing you love will ever be lost
it says what's held dearest apart from the self can be lost; the self can't be.

games.q: a friend's phone, with every photo on it, falls in a lake. she says, 'it's like i lost myself.' what would this verse gently say?
o: the photos mattered, and the one who loved those days is still here.
the photos never mattered at all, so don't be sad.
she did lose her self; it was stored on the phone.
games.why: things held dear can be lost, the text says honestly. the innermost self, the one who loved them, isn't among them; it's what made them dear.

practice: Yajnavalkya ends his answer to Maitreyi with a practice: the self is to be heard, reflected on, and meditated on. Try the middle one, reflecting.

Think of one thing you'll have to leave behind this year, and ask Maitreyi's question of it, quietly: would this make me deathless? Then think of one person you love, and turn the love around: where is it coming from?
Rest there while the breath comes and goes.

wordCard.voice: Aham brahmasmi, and its self as the dearest: innermost, dearer than a son, than wealth, than all else; the self Maitreyi asked to be taught.

orig.note: Sanskrit preyah, dearer: the self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than all else.

carryVoice: Your line: the innermost self is dearest of all. What's innermost can't be left on the curb. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.8 (this self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than all else, and is innermost; if one says to someone who holds another thing dearer than the self, 'you will lose what you hold dear', it may well happen; one should hold the self alone as dear; for one who does, what is dear does not perish)

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.1–5 (Yajnavalkya, about to leave household life, offers to divide his property; Maitreyi asks whether the earth full of wealth would make her immortal; no, her life would be like that of the wealthy; what would she do with what does not make her immortal? not for love of the husband is the husband dear, but for love of the self; so for sons and wealth; the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on); retold at 4.5
